passage.sceneTitle: The Boy in the Apple Barrel
passage.preamble: Jim Hawkins is a boy at sea on a ship called the Hispaniola, sailing to hunt for buried treasure. The ship's cook, Long John Silver, has always been friendly to him and has flattered him more than once.

numberedLines.text: Now, just after sundown, when all my work was over and I was on my way to my berth, it
occurred to me that I should like an apple. I ran on deck. The watch was all forward
looking out for the island. The man at the helm was watching the luff of the sail and
whistling away gently to himself, and that was the only sound excepting the swish of the
sea against the bows and around the sides of the ship.
In I got bodily into the apple barrel, and found there was scarce an apple left; but
sitting down there in the dark, what with the sound of the waters and the rocking
movement of the ship, I had either fallen asleep or was on the point of doing so when a
heavy man sat down with rather a clash close by. The barrel shook as he leaned his
shoulders against it, and I was just about to jump up when the man began to speak. It
was Silver’s voice, and before I had heard a dozen words, I would not have shown myself
for all the world, but lay there, trembling and listening, in the extreme of fear and
curiosity, for from these dozen words I understood that the lives of all the honest men
aboard depended upon me alone.
You may imagine how I felt when I heard this abominable old rogue addressing another in
the very same words of flattery as he had used to myself. Meantime, he ran on, little
supposing he was overheard.
“Here it is about gentlemen of fortune. They lives rough, and they risk swinging, but
they eat and drink like fighting-cocks, and when a cruise is done, why, it’s hundreds of
pounds instead of hundreds of farthings in their pockets. Now, the most goes for rum and
a good fling, and to sea again in their shirts. But that’s not the course I lay. I puts
it all away, some here, some there, and none too much anywheres, by reason of suspicion.
I’m fifty, mark you; once back from this cruise, I set up gentleman in earnest. Time
enough too, says you. Ah, but I’ve lived easy in the meantime, never denied myself o’
nothing heart desires, and slep’ soft and ate dainty all my days but when at sea. And
how did I begin? Before the mast, like you!”
“Well, I tell you now,” replied the lad, “I didn’t half a quarter like the job till I
had this talk with you, John; but there’s my hand on it now.”
“And a brave lad you were, and smart too,” answered Silver, shaking hands so heartily
that all the barrel shook, “and a finer figurehead for a gentleman of fortune I never
clapped my eyes on.”
By this time I had begun to understand the meaning of their terms. By a “gentleman of
fortune” they plainly meant neither more nor less than a common pirate, and the little
scene that I had overheard was the last act in the corruption of one of the honest hands
--perhaps of the last one left aboard. But on this point I was soon to be relieved, for
Silver giving a little whistle, a third man strolled up and sat down by the party.
“Dick’s square,” said Silver.
“Oh, I know’d Dick was square,” returned the voice of the coxswain, Israel Hands. “He’s
no fool, is Dick.” And he turned his quid and spat. “But look here,” he went on, “here’s
what I want to know, Barbecue: how long are we a-going to stand off and on like a
blessed bumboat? I’ve had a’most enough o’ Cap’n Smollett; he’s hazed me long enough, by
thunder! I want to go into that cabin, I do. I want their pickles and wines, and that.”
“When! By the powers!” cried Silver. “Well now, if you want to know, I’ll tell you when.
The last moment I can manage, and that’s when. Here’s a first-rate seaman, Cap’n
Smollett, sails the blessed ship for us. Here’s this squire and doctor with a map and
such--I don’t know where it is, do I? No more do you, says you. Well then, I mean this
squire and doctor shall find the stuff, and help us to get it aboard, by the powers.
Then we’ll see. If I was sure of you all, sons of double Dutchmen, I’d have Cap’n
Smollett navigate us half-way back again before I struck.”
“Dick!” he added, breaking off. “You just jump up, like a sweet lad, and get me an
apple, to wet my pipe like.”
You may fancy the terror I was in! I should have leaped out and run for it if I had
found the strength, but my limbs and heart alike misgave me. I heard Dick begin to rise,
and then someone seemingly stopped him, and the voice of Hands exclaimed, “Oh, stow
that! Don’t you get sucking of that bilge, John. Let’s have a go of the rum.”
“Dick,” said Silver, “I trust you. I’ve a gauge on the keg, mind. There’s the key; you
fill a pannikin and bring it up.”
Just then a sort of brightness fell upon me in the barrel, and looking up, I found the
moon had risen and was silvering the mizzen-top and shining white on the luff of the
fore-sail; and almost at the same time the voice of the lookout shouted, “Land ho!”

stem.text: Look at lines 1 to 5. Why did Jim run on deck?

rows.key: He had taken a fancy for an apple.

options.value: He had taken a fancy for an apple.
His work for the day was over.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True at line 1, and it says when he was free rather than why he went.

options.value: He was looking out for the island.
options.tagChildHint: Ask what exactly made this happen. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: Lines 2 and 3 give that to the watch, not to Jim.

options.value: He could not settle down in his berth.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: A boy at sea might not settle; lines 1 to 5 never say it.

rows.hintCore: Ask what sent him, not what let him go.
rows.walkScript: Line 1 says his work was over and he was heading to his berth. Line 2 gives the reason he turned round: he would like an apple. The watch, not Jim, was forward looking out for the island.

There was straw packed round the apples.

options.execution: Barrels are packed that way; lines 6 to 9 never say so.

options.value: The moon was shining white on the sail.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: True at line 59, far outside this window; lines 6 to 9 are in the dark.

rows.hintCore: Find what was there, not who arrived.
rows.walkScript: Line 6 says he got bodily into the barrel and looked. The same line says there was scarce an apple left. The man who sits down comes after, at line 9.

options.value: He was just about to jump up.

stem.text: Look at lines 15 to 17. What does 'rogue' on line 15 mean here?

rows.key: A man who cannot be trusted.

options.value: A man with a rough manner.
options.tagChildHint: This word looks like one you know. Read it letter by letter and check it is the same word.
options.execution: Takes the meaning from rough, a word it resembles in form.

options.value: A playful person who teases.
options.tagChildHint: More than one meaning fits this word. Find the words nearby that decide which one it has to be.
options.execution: A real sense of the word; line 15 fixes the harsher one.

options.value: A man who repeats his own words.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True at lines 15 and 16, and it answers what Silver does rather than what rogue means.

options.value: A man who cannot be trusted.

rows.hintCore: Look at what Silver is doing in the next two lines.
rows.walkScript: Line 15 calls Silver an old rogue, right after Jim hears him. Lines 16 and 17 show him flattering a second boy in the very same words. So rogue names a man who cannot be trusted.

stem.text: Look at lines 18 to 26 and 43 to 49. How do Silver's two speeches differ?

rows.key: First he talks of his own money, then of using other men.

options.value: First he talks of his own money, then of using other men.
First he says the life is rough, then he says the pay is good.
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: Reuses lines 18 and 19, and both halves come from the first speech alone.

options.value: First he calls Dick square, then he trusts him with the keg.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: True at line 37 and at line 56, both outside the two windows named here. In the window, line 22 answers the stem: 'it all away, some here, some there, and none'.

options.value: First he spends all he earns, then he puts a little away.
options.tagChildHint: Some words tell you how two things go together. Find that word and read it again.
options.execution: Lines 20 to 22 say the opposite: the most goes for rum, and he puts it all away.

rows.hintCore: Ask who or what each speech is really about.
rows.walkScript: Line 22 has him put his own money away, some here, some there. Lines 45 to 47 have the squire and doctor find the stuff for him. The first speech is about his money, the second about other men.

stem.text: Look at lines 27 to 31. What has the talk with Silver done to the lad?

rows.key: It has won him over to the job at last.

options.value: He liked the job from the very start.
options.tagChildHint: A negative word can change the whole answer. Read the line again for one.
options.execution: Lines 27 and 28 say he did not half a quarter like it until the talk.

options.value: It has won him over to the job at last.
It has made Silver shake his hand hard.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True at lines 29 and 30, and it answers what Silver did rather than what changed in the lad.

options.value: Silver praised him, so he agreed to join.
options.tagChildHint: Check what happened first, and what the question asks for.
options.execution: The praise at line 29 comes after the hand at line 28, so the cause sits later than the effect.

rows.hintCore: Read the small word that turns the sentence around.
rows.walkScript: Line 27 says he did not half a quarter like the job at first. Line 28 says that changed after the talk with Silver. Line 28 gives his hand on it, so he is won over.

stem.text: Look at lines 52 and 53. What does 'misgave' on line 53 mean here?

options.value: They would not do as he wanted them to.

options.tagChildHint: More than one meaning fits this word. Find the words nearby that decide which one it has to be.
options.execution: Misgive can mean to fill with doubt; line 53 fixes the sense of giving way.

options.value: He would have leaped out and run for it.

options.execution: True at line 52, and it states what he wanted rather than the meaning of the word.

rows.walkScript: Line 52 says he would have leaped out if he had found the strength. Line 53 says his limbs and heart alike misgave him. So they gave way and would not carry him.

options.value: His body cannot move, but his mind goes on working things out.

rows.hintCore: Watch him from the first line to the last. He does not move.
rows.walkScript: At line 10 he means to jump up, and instead he lies there trembling. At lines 32 and 33 he cannot move, yet he works out what their terms mean. At line 53 his limbs give way while his ears keep gathering the plot.
